body:
Understanding drought

A drought is a prolonged period during which water availability becomes unusually deficient in relation to normal conditions or requirements. In many cases, the initial cause is inadequate rainfall. High evaporation, increased water demand and the depletion of stored water can intensify its effects.

Unlike a flash flood, drought usually develops gradually. Its effects may continue even after rainfall resumes because reservoirs, groundwater, soils and livelihoods do not necessarily recover immediately.

Drought is not the same as ordinary seasonal dryness. A region may have a predictably dry summer every year without experiencing a drought. Drought refers to an abnormal or consequential shortage relative to the region's usual water conditions and needs.

Aridity is a long-term climatic characteristic; drought is a temporary departure or period of water deficiency. An arid region can experience drought, but a normally humid region can also suffer drought when rainfall or available water becomes unusually inadequate.

Three principal types of drought

TypeMeaningWhat is observed?
Meteorological droughtRainfall or precipitation remains substantially below the expected pattern for the area and period.Rainfall deficit, prolonged dry spells or abnormal distribution of rainfall.
Agricultural droughtSoil moisture is insufficient to meet crop requirements during important growth stages.Dry root-zone soil, crop stress, poor growth or reduced yield.
Hydrological droughtWater in rivers, reservoirs, lakes or groundwater systems becomes unusually deficient.Low streamflow, reduced reservoir storage or falling groundwater levels.

How the types are related

A prolonged rainfall deficit can first become apparent in meteorological records. If the soil dries and crops cannot obtain sufficient moisture, agricultural drought may develop. If the shortage persists, river flow, reservoir levels and groundwater availability may decline, producing hydrological drought.

This sequence is common but not compulsory. The timing and severity depend on soil, crop type, irrigation, existing reservoir storage, groundwater use and the timing of rainfall. A short dry spell at a critical crop stage can cause agricultural damage even when seasonal rainfall is not exceptionally low. Conversely, irrigation may protect some crops from a rainfall shortage while groundwater reserves continue to decline.

Examples that distinguish the types

  • A district receives substantially less monsoon rainfall than its long-term normal. This is evidence relevant to meteorological drought.
  • Rainfall stops during a critical crop-growth stage, leaving insufficient moisture around plant roots. This indicates agricultural drought, even if some rain fell earlier.
  • A prolonged shortage reduces reservoir levels and groundwater availability, restricting supplies. This indicates hydrological drought.

Why drought becomes a livelihood disaster

Water scarcity may reduce crop production, drinking-water availability and fodder supplies. Farmers may lose income, agricultural labourers may find less employment, and livestock owners may struggle to obtain feed and water. Falling incomes can affect food security and contribute to distress migration.

Water scarcity can also create public-health risks when people are forced to depend on unsafe sources. Thus, drought is not only a meteorological event; it can become an agricultural, economic, social and public-health problem.

Gujarat's contrasting conditions

Kachchh and parts of Saurashtra and northern Gujarat are especially sensitive to rainfall variability and water scarcity. Agriculture in rain-dependent areas is vulnerable to delayed monsoon onset, long breaks in rainfall and inadequate soil moisture. Yet the same state may experience heavy rain and flooding elsewhere, or even flooding in a drought-prone region during a different period.

The important geographic lesson is that flood risk and drought risk are not mutually exclusive. Both can arise from the uneven distribution of monsoon rainfall over time and space.

Prelims focus

  • Meteorological drought concerns deficient precipitation.
  • Agricultural drought concerns inadequate soil moisture for crops.
  • Hydrological drought concerns deficient rivers, reservoirs, lakes or groundwater.
  • Hydrological drought may continue after rainfall begins to recover.
  • Aridity describes a long-term climatic condition, unlike a drought episode.
  • Trap: A normal seasonal rainfall total does not by itself rule out damaging dry spells during crop growth.

[Sources: NCERT, India: Physical Environment, Class 11, 2026–27, Chapter 6, Natural Hazards and Disasters, printed pp. 64–66; Government of India, Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, Manual for Drought Management, December 2016, Chapter 1, Understanding Drought; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12, Chapter 5, Land Resources and Agriculture, sections on rainfed farming and agricultural problems.]

title: Drought: Meaning, Meteorological, Agricultural and Hydrological Types

body:
Why rainfall alone is not enough

A drought assessment must determine both whether rainfall has been deficient and whether that deficiency is affecting water supplies, crops and livelihoods. Rainfall is the starting point for many assessments, but 2 districts with similar rainfall deficits can experience different consequences because they have different soils, irrigation systems, groundwater reserves and crop patterns.

India's Manual for Drought Management, 2016 recommends combining rainfall information with agricultural, vegetation and hydrological indicators rather than relying on a single observation.

Important drought indicators and indices

IndicatorWhat it measuresHow to interpret it
Rainfall departureDifference between observed rainfall and the long-term normal.Below-normal rainfall may indicate developing meteorological drought.
Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI)Precipitation anomaly expressed on a standardized scale.Negative values indicate drier-than-normal conditions for the assessed period and location.
Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI)Vegetation greenness inferred from satellite observations.Abnormally poor vegetation condition can support evidence of agricultural stress.
Soil-moisture indicatorsWater available in the soil.Low moisture may indicate agricultural drought.
Reservoir and groundwater indicatorsStored surface water and groundwater conditions.Unusually depleted storage supports assessment of hydrological drought.
Streamflow indicatorsWater flowing through rivers and streams.Unusually low flow can indicate hydrological drought.

Understanding SPI correctly

SPI stands for Standardized Precipitation Index. It uses historical precipitation records to express how unusual the rainfall of a particular period is for a location. Because it standardizes precipitation, it can help compare unusually wet or dry conditions across places with different rainfall climates.

A negative SPI indicates less precipitation than the reference conditions; a positive value indicates wetter conditions. The magnitude of the departure matters: a small negative value is not equivalent to an extreme drought.

The Government of India's 2016 Manual gives the following dry categories:

SPI rangeCategory in the 2016 Manual
-1.0 to -1.49Moderately dry
-1.5 to -1.99Severely dry
Below -2.0Extremely dry

These are index categories, not automatic proof that every affected administrative area must be officially declared drought-affected. Actual declaration also considers impact information and verification.

NDVI and crop-condition assessment

NDVI uses satellite measurements to help assess the condition of vegetation. Healthy growing vegetation generally produces a different spectral response from sparse or stressed vegetation. A decline in greenness compared with an appropriate normal period may indicate crop stress.

However, NDVI cannot identify drought independently in every situation. Harvesting, changes in crop type, the normal agricultural calendar and land-cover differences can also change vegetation greenness. A meaningful comparison therefore uses an appropriate seasonal and local reference.

How the 2016 drought-assessment framework works

The 2016 Manual describes a multi-stage assessment. Rainfall-related information, such as rainfall departure, SPI or prolonged dry spells, provides the initial trigger. Impact indicators are then examined, including crop area, remote-sensing vegetation condition, soil moisture and hydrology.

For impact assessment, the Manual describes using information from 3 of the 4 groups of agricultural, vegetation, soil-moisture and hydrological indicators. Sample field verification, also called ground truthing, helps determine whether remotely observed or statistical conditions reflect actual hardship.

The Manual identifies the State Government as the authority that issues a drought declaration through a notification specifying the affected administrative areas and severity. State departments then coordinate the response. The 2016 document is a dated government guidance framework; its specific administrative norms should not be mistaken for an independently verified account of every later amendment.

No single rainfall-deficit percentage establishes all forms of drought. A rainfall indicator may trigger closer assessment, while actual agricultural, hydrological and livelihood impacts determine how serious the shortage has become.

Why field information matters

Scientific indices are useful because drought can develop across large areas and over long periods. Yet a satellite image may not capture a household's lack of drinking water, the price of fodder or the loss of agricultural employment. Such information is important for assessing livelihood distress and directing assistance where it is needed.

Prelims focus

  • SPI is based on precipitation, not directly on crop yield or groundwater.
  • Negative SPI values indicate drier-than-normal conditions.
  • NDVI is a vegetation-condition indicator derived from satellite observations.
  • Reservoir, groundwater and streamflow information supports hydrological drought assessment.
  • The 2016 Drought Manual combines rainfall triggers, impact indicators and ground truthing.
  • Trap: A low NDVI value alone does not establish that drought caused the vegetation condition.

[Sources: Government of India, Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, Manual for Drought Management, December 2016, Chapter 3, sections 3.1–3.4, especially Table 3.2 and the drought-determination matrix; NCERT, India: Physical Environment, Class 11, 2026–27, Chapter 6, pp. 64–66. The official 2016 Manual was consulted on 2 November 2026.]

title: Drought Monitoring: Rainfall Indices, Vegetation Signals and Official Assessment

body:
Preparedness must begin before water becomes scarce

Drought management includes measures taken before a shortage, adjustments made when rainfall becomes deficient and relief provided when households or livelihoods are affected. Because drought usually develops gradually, monitoring and early action can reduce losses.

A useful starting point is a local water budget: an understanding of available rainfall, stored water, expected demands and the likely period of scarcity. This is not merely a calculation of annual rainfall. Drinking water, livestock needs, crops, industries and natural ecosystems may all depend on the same limited supplies.

Protecting water availability

  • Rainwater harvesting: Collecting and storing suitable rainfall runoff can increase water available for later use.
  • Watershed management: Protecting vegetation, soils and local drainage helps conserve soil moisture, reduce erosion and support water availability.
  • Groundwater recharge: Appropriate recharge measures can help replenish aquifers where local geological and water-quality conditions permit.
  • Efficient irrigation: Drip and sprinkler systems can reduce some forms of water loss compared with poorly managed surface irrigation.
  • Water reuse: Properly treated water can be reused for suitable purposes, reducing pressure on freshwater sources.
  • Demand management: Preventing leakage, avoiding unnecessary water use and matching irrigation to crop needs help extend limited supplies.

Water-conservation measures have different effects. A check dam or storage pond may hold runoff locally, whereas drip irrigation principally improves the efficiency with which water reaches crops. Neither produces rainfall. Their value lies in using the water that is available more effectively.

Agricultural planning for uncertain monsoons

Rainfed agriculture depends mainly on rainfall rather than assured irrigation. Its vulnerability increases when rain arrives late, is poorly distributed or stops during important crop-growth stages.

Farmers and agricultural agencies can reduce risk by matching crops and sowing decisions to the available soil moisture and expected rainfall. Measures include selecting suitable crop varieties, adjusting sowing dates when advised, conserving soil moisture through mulching and using locally appropriate intercropping or crop diversification.

Some relatively drought-tolerant crops, including bajra and certain pulses, are important in drier agricultural regions. Drought tolerance does not mean that a crop can grow without water; it means that the crop may withstand particular periods of moisture stress better than a more water-demanding alternative.

When the expected monsoon fails or is delayed, a crop contingency plan provides alternative sowing and crop-management options suited to local rainfall conditions. The appropriate plan depends on the season, remaining growing period and available resources.

Distinguishing agricultural protection from emergency relief

ApproachPurposeExamples
Long-term risk reductionMake water use and livelihoods less vulnerable to recurring shortages.Watershed conservation, suitable crops, efficient irrigation and water storage.
Early responseReduce losses when deficient rainfall or water stress begins to appear.Crop contingency advice, monitoring water supplies and prioritising essential needs.
Relief and livelihood supportAssist affected people and animals during serious scarcity.Safe drinking water, fodder arrangements, eligible financial assistance and livelihood support.

Livelihoods and public-health needs

The impact of drought extends beyond the farmer whose crop fails. Agricultural labourers may lose work, livestock owners may face rising fodder costs, and families may spend more time or money obtaining drinking water. These effects can be particularly severe for households with little savings or alternative income.

Relief therefore needs to consider safe drinking water, food security, fodder, livestock water, essential health services and livelihood support. Employment or financial assistance may be provided under applicable government schemes, subject to their eligibility rules and the relevant official decisions.

Preparedness can begin before a formal drought notification where signs of distress are already evident. A formal declaration is important for activating particular relief provisions, but routine monitoring, crop advice and water conservation need not wait for a crisis.

Application to Gujarat

In parts of Kachchh, Saurashtra and northern Gujarat, irregular monsoon rainfall makes local water storage, groundwater management, soil-moisture conservation and suitable rainfed cropping especially relevant. Water available from a river or reservoir may support a region during a dry period, but excessive dependence on a single source can also create vulnerability.

Protection of essential drinking-water supplies and careful groundwater use are therefore as important as measures intended to save an individual agricultural season.

Prelims focus

  • Rainwater harvesting stores or conserves rainfall for later use.
  • Drip irrigation improves the efficiency of water application to crops.
  • Crop contingency planning provides alternatives when expected rainfall fails.
  • Drought-tolerant crops still require water.
  • Drought relief may address drinking water, fodder, livelihoods and health.
  • Trap: Increasing groundwater extraction can temporarily meet demand but may worsen longer-term water scarcity.

[Sources: NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8, Chapter 2, printed pp. 14–17, 2018–19 reprint; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12, Chapter 5, Land Resources and Agriculture, sections on rainfed farming and agricultural problems, and Chapter 6, Water Resources, printed pp. 60–65; NCERT, India: Physical Environment, Class 11, 2026–27, Chapter 6, pp. 64–66; Government of India, Manual for Drought Management, December 2016, Chapter 4, Drought Response and Relief.]
